In 1056, according to Burmese chronicles, King Anawrahta of Pagan adopted Theravada Buddhism, the "teaching of the elders", and made it the religion of his kingdom. From Pagan it spread across mainland Southeast Asia.

The chronicles tell it this way. A Mon monk, Shin Arahan, came from the south and converted the king. Anawrahta asked the Mon king of Thaton for copies of the Pali scriptures and was refused, so in 1057 he conquered Thaton and carried off its monks, texts and craftsmen to Pagan. Historians now doubt parts of this story, and Buddhism of several kinds was present in Upper Burma long before, among the Pyu. But the turn toward Theravada under Anawrahta is well established.

What followed:

  • Anawrahta built the Shwezigon pagoda and began the building boom that filled the plain of Bagan with temples.
  • Pagan kept close ties with Sri Lanka, the main centre of Theravada, exchanging monks and texts and helping its king restore the order of monks there.
  • Burmese monks later reformed their order on the Sri Lankan model.

Over the next centuries Theravada became the faith of the Thai kingdoms of Sukhothai and Ayutthaya, of Laos, and of Cambodia, where it replaced the Hindu and Mahayana cults of the Khmer Empire. Today it is the main religion of Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Sri Lanka, a map whose Burmese part starts at Pagan.
sum: In 1056, according to Burmese chronicles, King Anawrahta of Pagan adopted Theravada Buddhism, the "teaching of the elders", and made it the religion of his kingdom. From Pagan it spread across mainland Southeast Asia.
